name: Scaling an AI-Powered Business
objectives: Given six months of business numbers with customer names removed, track five key numbers in a spreadsheet and use AI to explain the trends, checking AI's math and saying whether each sale is profitable

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Knowing your key numbers
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Track five key numbers and use AI to explain what they mean.
This lesson builds toward: Given six months of business numbers with customer names removed, you will track five key numbers in a spreadsheet and use AI to explain the trends, checking AI's math and saying whether each sale is profitable.
You cannot grow what you do not measure. Five numbers matter for most small businesses: monthly revenue (money in), costs, profit (what is left), number of customers, and how much each customer is worth over time compared with what it costs to get them.
Put the last six months in a spreadsheet. Then ask AI to help you read it: "Here are my monthly revenue, costs and customer counts (no names). What trends do you see? Which number should I worry about?" Check its math yourself.
A business is ready to scale when each sale makes a profit and customers keep coming back or recommend you. If each sale loses money, growing makes the loss bigger.
Step by step:
- Make a spreadsheet with six months of revenue, costs, profit and customer count.
- Work out average sale and cost to get a customer.
- Ask AI to describe trends and risks (no customer names).
- Redo any calculations yourself.
- Write one sentence: is each sale profitable?
Words to know:
- Revenue: all the money that comes in from sales.
- Profit: revenue minus costs.
- Customer acquisition cost: what you spend, on average, to get one new customer.
- Scale: grow sales faster than costs and effort.
Try it now: Build your six-month numbers sheet, ask AI to point out trends and one risk, check its math, and write whether each sale is profitable.
You can now track your key numbers and judge whether your business is ready to scale.

options: What you spend on average to get one new customer
The number of customers you have
check.why: It shows how much each new customer costs you to win.

check.q: AI says your profit doubled last month, but it feels wrong. What do you do?
options: Check the math yourself in the spreadsheet
Ask AI to say it again
check.why: Always check AI's math before acting on it.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Finding the bottleneck
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Find the one step that most limits how much your business can handle.
This lesson builds toward: Given the steps of your main process with times, you will identify the bottleneck and choose one fix: remove, automate or hand off, with the fix ready to try this month.
A bottleneck is the narrowest point that limits everything else. In a cake business it might be oven space; in a service business it is often the owner's time for quotes, follow-up or quality checks.
List the steps from first contact to happy customer and how long each takes per customer. Ask AI: "Here are my steps and times. Where is the bottleneck, and what are three ways to fix it: remove the step, automate it, or hand it off?"
Fix the bottleneck first. Speeding up any other step does not help, because work still piles up at the narrow point.
Step by step:
- List each step from first contact to finished job.
- Write the time each step takes per customer and who does it.
- Ask AI to find the bottleneck and suggest fixes.
- Choose remove, automate or hand off.
- Plan one fix to try in the next month.
Words to know:
- Bottleneck: the slowest step, which limits how much the whole business can do.
- Hand off: give a task to someone else to do.
Try it now: Write your steps with times, ask AI to find the bottleneck, and choose one fix (remove, automate or hand off) to try this month.
You can now find the step that limits your growth and pick a fix.

options: The slowest step that limits everything else
check.why: Work piles up at the bottleneck, so it limits growth.

check.q: Every quote waits for you to write it, and orders pile up. What fix could you choose?
options: Use a quote template or hand quoting to a trained helper
check.why: Automating or handing off the bottleneck step frees up the flow.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Turning your work into systems
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Document two key jobs as systems someone else (or an AI tool) can run.
This lesson builds toward: Given two key jobs you do yourself, you will write each as a system with steps, a checklist and a quality standard, so someone else can follow it without asking questions.
If everything lives in your head, the business cannot grow past you. A system is a written way of doing a job: the steps, the tools, the checklist and what "done well" looks like.
Record yourself doing a job, or write rough notes, and ask AI to turn it into a standard operating procedure (SOP) with a checklist and a quality standard. Mark which steps AI tools can do and where a person must check.
Test each system by having someone else follow it while you watch quietly. Every question they ask shows a missing step. Keep systems in one shared place.
Step by step:
- Pick the two jobs that take most of your time.
- Record or write notes while you do each one.
- Ask AI to turn the notes into an SOP with a checklist and quality standard.
- Mark AI steps and human checks.
- Test with another person and fill the gaps.
Words to know:
- System: a written, repeatable way of doing a job.
- SOP: standard operating procedure: the written steps for a job.
- Quality standard: a clear description of what good work looks like.
Try it now: Turn one of your two biggest jobs into an SOP with AI's help, including a checklist and a quality standard. Have someone test it if you can.
You can now turn your know-how into systems that others or AI tools can run.

check.q: What is a quality standard in an SOP?
options: A clear description of what a good result looks like
check.why: A quality standard tells the person what done well means.

check.q: A helper keeps calling you with questions while following your SOP. What do you do?
options: Add the missing details to the SOP and test it again
check.why: Questions show where the SOP is not yet complete.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Bringing on help: people and AI tools
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Decide what help to add and prepare a role description.
This lesson builds toward: Given the help your business needs most, you will choose between an AI tool and a person and prepare a fair role description, with job-related wording and a note on worker status using the IRS's three categories.
Some work is best handed to an AI tool or automation (sorting, drafting, scheduling). Some needs a person (judgment, hands-on work, customer relationships). Use your bottleneck and systems to decide which.
If you hire a person, AI can draft a clear role description from your SOPs: tasks, skills, hours and pay range. Check it for fair, inclusive wording and remove anything unrelated to the job.
Contractor or employee? The IRS looks at three kinds of evidence: behavioral control (do you control how the work is done?), financial control (who controls pay, expenses and tools?) and the type of relationship (contracts, benefits, ongoing and central work). Getting this wrong can cost you taxes and penalties; read the IRS page, and ask an accountant or lawyer. State rules can be stricter.
Step by step:
- List the work you want off your plate.
- Mark each: AI tool, contractor or employee.
- Have AI draft a role description from your SOPs.
- Check the wording for fairness and remove unrelated requirements.
- Read the IRS worker-status page and ask an accountant before hiring.
Words to know:
- Contractor: someone in business for themselves who does work for you, usually controlling how they do it.
- Employee: someone whose work you control; you withhold and pay employment taxes.
- Role description: a written summary of a job's tasks, skills, hours and pay.
Official sources:
- IRS: Independent Contractor (Self-Employed) or Employee?
Try it now: Choose the help you need most. If it is a person, have AI draft a role description from your SOP and check it for fairness; note whether you think it is a contractor or employee role and why, using the IRS's three categories.
You can now decide between AI tools and people for growth, and prepare a fair role description.

check.q: Which job usually needs a person rather than AI?
check.why: Relationships need human judgment and trust.

check.q: AI's role description says "young, energetic team member". What do you do?
options: Change it to fair, job-related wording
check.why: Role descriptions should be fair and about the job.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Growing customers step by step
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Choose one growth channel and design a small, measurable test.
This lesson builds toward: Given possible growth channels, you will plan a 30-day test of one channel with a target, a measure and a spending limit, comparing cost per new customer with your key numbers.
Growth channels are the ways new customers find you: referrals, partnerships, local search and maps listings, social media, email, paid ads, marketplaces. Most small businesses grow best through one or two channels done well.
Ask AI: "My business is [type] serving [customer]. Suggest five growth channels, how each would work for me, what it would cost, and how I would measure it." Pick the one that fits your customer and budget.
Run a small test for 30 days with a clear target: "Ask 20 past customers for referrals; goal: 5 new leads." Measure the result, compare the cost per new customer with your numbers from Lesson 1, and only then spend more.
Step by step:
- Ask AI for five possible growth channels with costs and measures.
- Pick one that fits your customer and budget.
- Set a 30-day test with a clear target.
- Track results and cost per new customer.
- Decide: grow it, change it or stop it.
Words to know:
- Growth channel: a way new customers find and buy from you.
- Referral: a customer recommending you to someone else.
- Test: a small, time-limited try with a clear target.
Try it now: Choose one growth channel with AI's help and write a 30-day test: what you will do, the target, how you will measure it, and the most you will spend.
You can now pick a growth channel and test it before spending more.

check.q: What does a good 30-day growth test include?
options: A clear target and a spending limit
check.why: A target and a limit tell you whether the channel works without big risk.

check.q: Your test brings in customers, but each costs more than they are worth to you. What do you do?
options: Stop or change the channel before spending more
check.why: Compare cost per new customer with customer value before scaling a channel.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping quality as you grow
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Set weekly quality checks and a plan for AI and data risks as you grow.
This lesson builds toward: For your 90-day scaling plan, you will set three weekly quality checks and a review of AI tools and customer data, reviewing the plan every two weeks.
Growth often breaks quality: rushed work, slower replies, AI drafts that nobody checks. Choose three quality numbers to watch weekly, such as average review rating, reply time, and redo or refund rate.
As more work runs through AI tools, risks grow too: more customer data in more tools, more AI content going out. Review which tools hold customer data, who has access, and that a person still checks anything customers see.
Put it together in a 90-day plan. Ask AI to help you lay it out, but every number and date should be one you believe. Review it every two weeks and adjust.
Step by step:
- Choose three quality numbers to track weekly.
- List which tools hold customer data and who can access them.
- Confirm a human checks everything customers see.
- Ask AI to lay out your 90-day plan from your notes.
- Set a review every two weeks.
Words to know:
- Quality check: a regular look at a number or sample of work to make sure standards hold.
- Refund rate: the share of sales you had to give money back on.
Try it now: Final task: write your one-page 90-day scaling plan: key numbers and targets, bottleneck fix, two systems, the help you will add, one growth test, and three weekly quality checks.
You can now plan and manage growth with AI while protecting quality and customer data.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Key numbers Fewer than five numbers, no targets, or AI's math not checked. Five key numbers today with 90-day targets, math checked. Says clearly whether each sale is profitable and why. Bottleneck fix No bottleneck named, or the fix is vague. The main bottleneck and one fix: remove, automate or hand off. Shows step times that prove it is the bottleneck. Systems Fewer than two systems, or missing steps or a quality standard. Two systems named, each with steps, a checklist and a quality standard. At least one was tested by someone else. Help and growth test No cost for the help, or the growth test has no target or limit. The help to add with its cost, and one growth test with a target, measure and limit. Worker status noted with the IRS categories, and a plan to compare cost per new customer. Quality checks Fewer than three checks, or no review date. Three weekly quality checks and a review every two weeks. Also includes a check on which AI tools hold customer data. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which is a weekly quality number?
check.why: Redo and refund rates show whether quality is slipping.

check.q: Sales are growing, but complaints doubled this month. What does your plan tell you to do?
options: Find the cause and fix it before adding more customers
check.why: Quality checks exist so growth does not break what customers love.
